messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Boun had spent forty years as a roofer, his body attuned to the sun and the specific balance required to move across a steep pitch. At sixty-six, he was still strong, the man his family relied on. That changed eight months ago, on a hot afternoon re-sealing the roof of a small manufacturing plant. A pressure valve on an exhaust stack released with a violent hiss, bathing him in a plume of acrid, invisible chemicals. The world tilted, his lungs burned, and he remembers a frantic scramble away from the vent before his vision narrowed and the paramedics were looking down at him. The next clear memory was the sterile, antiseptic smell of the hospital, a scent that now clung to him like a shroud.

In the first few weeks home, the event replayed itself relentlessly. It wasn't just a memory; it was a film, vivid and detailed, that would start without warning—the hiss of the valve, the dizzying view of the ground, the burning in his chest. When these memories ambushed him, Boun would retreat into himself, trying desperately to push the images away while simultaneously dwelling on the man he used to be before the accident, a man who wasn't afraid of the sky. Sometimes, even more unsettlingly, the terror would arrive without a picture; he would be sitting at the dinner table and suddenly feel the full, suffocating emotional intensity of the event, his heart hammering for a reason his mind couldn't see.

Soon, the world began to fill with invisible tripwires. The sharp smell of his wife’s cleaning ammonia would send him reeling back to the rooftop, sparking the memory reel and an immediate, frantic effort to suppress it. A routine doctor’s visit became an ordeal; the hospital smell in the waiting room was enough to make him feel profoundly unsafe, a suffocating sense that danger was imminent and he was unable to relax. This pervasive sense of threat began to bleed into everything. When he felt this agitated and on edge, he found the vivid memories of the accident were even more likely to break through his defenses. To manage the feeling, he started avoiding any place he didn't know, turning down his son’s invitations to new restaurants because he couldn’t assess the danger in an unfamiliar layout.

This retreat inward solidified into a devastating cycle. Waking up in the pitch-black of night became a recurring terror. The darkness itself was a trigger, plunging him into a state of high alert that made sleep impossible. He would lie there, rigid and unable to relax, convinced that some unseen threat was gathering. To cope, he would try to force the thoughts from his mind, a strategy that only made him feel weaker when it failed. This failure fed a growing, painful belief: he couldn't rely on himself anymore. This appraisal, that he was fundamentally broken and untrustworthy, became the lens through which he saw everything. It amplified his sense of ambient threat, making the world outside his home feel impossibly dangerous. His belief that danger was everywhere seemed to make him even more sensitive to the faintest chemical scent.

The more he saw the world as a dangerous place, the more he clung to his strategies of avoidance and suppression. He stopped disagreeing with his wife, even on small things, desperate to avoid any conflict that might tax his frayed nerves. He spent hours sitting silently, dwelling on his past strength, a habit that only highlighted his current feelings of hopelessness. Each time he tried and failed to suppress a memory, it was fresh evidence for his most painful conclusion: "I am not the man I was." The memory of his own helplessness on that roof directly fueled his appraisal that he was no longer capable. This conviction that he had no future, that he was permanently damaged, made him retreat further, avoiding people and places, which in turn reinforced the feeling that the world was hostile and he was right to fear it. His work, once a source of pride, was now a source of dread; he turned down any job on a commercial building, his income dwindling as his world shrank.

It was after he refused to attend his granddaughter’s fifth birthday party, held at a community hall he’d never been to, that his wife found him crying in the garage. The shame of his own fear was overwhelming. He came to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a desperate question: could he ever feel safe in his own home again, in his own mind? He feels he has no future, but he clings to the small, fading possibility of being a grandfather his family can rely on, even if he no longer believes he can rely on himself.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not explain how the patient's maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance) lead to increased sensitivity or the development of new triggers.
